claims.text: The target material is a crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticle composed of five or more metals.
Mo and Re are γ-partitioning elements suitable for minor alloying additions.
A minor Mo or Re addition can overcome nanoparticle instability during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
Minor additions of Mo or Re promote negative lattice misfit.
Negative lattice misfit promotes N-type rafting of γ′.
Minor additions of Mo or Re provide solid-solution strengthening to the γ matrix.
Adding Mo or Re causes formation of a stable solid solution in the nanoparticles.
Negative lattice misfit enhances the operational stability of the nanoparticle solid solution.
Negative lattice misfit improves catalytic performance.
Mo- or Re-modified nanoparticles will be more stable than untreated nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
Mo- or Re-modified nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than untreated nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
The proposed material can retain potential catalytic performance at low noble-metal content.
The proposed intervention applies across near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
Resistance to oxidation or corrosion is an appropriate measure of the claimed operational stability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is framed around a multielement solid solution, but N-type rafting requires distinct γ and γ′ phases and an interphase lattice misfit. This is not reconciled with the stated single-solid-solution architecture.
